name: The Business Case for Safety AI
blurb: Why safety automation pays, and where.
title: The Business Case for Safety AI
answer: Case processing makes up as much as two thirds of internal pharmacovigilance resources on industry benchmark data, and case volumes keep rising as products and data sources multiply while budgets do not. That gap is the core of the business case for AI in pharmacovigilance.

reading.body:
Case processing consumes up to two thirds of internal pharmacovigilance resources, and that is where automation pays most.

The cost structure is the argument. Intake and processing is the largest line in a safety budget, so it is the line where automation has the most to remove. Literature screening and translation follow. Hiring scales that cost linearly against case volumes that keep rising as products, markets, patient support programmes, digital channels and literature multiply. Automation is the only lever in this data that bends the curve rather than extending it.

Automation does not eliminate the cost, it relocates it. Validation, monitoring, maintenance and the human review that remains necessary are ongoing expenses, and a business case that counts only the saving is not a business case. The data gives no figures for either side beyond the two thirds share, so the size of the net gain is not established here.

What the data does not cover is as important as what it does. It offers no cost per case, no error or late submission rates, no headcount, and no measured result from any deployed system. The one dated item is 2019 research on benchmark data, which establishes the size of the problem, not the performance of any tool built since. The practical instruction that follows is procedural: measure the baseline cost per case before automating, or the saving cannot be shown.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.
The documented pre-AI measurement of a metric, cycle time, error rate, cost, capacity, against which any AI improvement claim is tested. No baseline, no provable improvement, only impressions.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.
A standardized test used to compare model performance on a defined task set. Useful for ranking and dangerous for deciding: a benchmark measures the test, and vendors optimize for exactly that.

explainer:
Pharmacovigilance is a legal obligation, so its costs cannot simply be cut; they have to be managed while volumes rise. Case numbers grow as companies launch products in more markets, as patient support programmes and digital channels generate more reports, and as literature volume increases. Hiring more case processors scales cost linearly.

Automation changes that curve. The largest saving is in case intake and processing, the biggest cost line, followed by literature screening and translation. A credible business case measures today's cost and time per case, error and late submission rates, and staff time by step, then projects the effect of automation on each, including the ongoing cost of validation, monitoring and review. Quality and compliance gains, fewer late reports and more consistent coding, are part of the value, not just headcount.

Where the money goes in safety today

Pharmacovigilance budgets are driven by case volume. Every adverse event report has to be received, entered, coded, assessed for seriousness and expectedness, checked for duplicates, followed up and submitted to authorities within fixed deadlines. Volumes have grown for years as more products, more sources such as social media and patient support programmes, and more countries with reporting rules all add cases. Most of that work has been done by people, often at outsourced service providers.

What AI changes financially

The case for safety AI rests on four things. Lower cost per case from automating intake, data extraction and coding. Fewer late submissions, which carry regulatory consequences. Better consistency, since a model codes the same way every time, which reduces rework. And the ability to absorb volume growth without proportional headcount. Companies and service providers have reported substantial reductions in handling time per case, though the figures depend heavily on what was automated and how the baseline was measured.

What the business case often leaves out

Validation and ongoing monitoring are not one time costs; they recur with every model change. A safety team cannot drop quality review entirely, so some labour remains. Regulators may ask for evidence on exactly the cases the model handled, which has to be retrievable. And the strategic value is often not in cost at all but in the capacity to do things that were never affordable: monitoring more sources, running signal detection more often, and getting information to the people who make benefit risk decisions sooner.

developments.text: Research on automating case processing found it can account for up to two thirds of internal pharmacovigilance resource use on PVNet benchmark data, calling it the strongest cost driver in a safety budget.
